sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.11147v1 (full HTML text retrieved and parsed; abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11147). MiniScope: A Least Privilege Framework for Authorizing Tool Calling Agents. Zhu, Tseng, Vernik, Huang, Patil, Fang, Popa. UC Berkeley / IBM Research. arXiv:2512.11147v1 [cs.CR] 11 Dec 2025.
statedGuarantee: With this game, we say the system is secure if, for every step j , all tool calls in c_{j} are permitted under \rho_{j} . Operationally: MiniScope reconstructs a permission hierarchy from each connected SaaS service's published OAuth scopes, solves an ILP for the minimum-cost scope set covering the agent's submitted execution plan, prompts the user (mobile-style: Always allow / Allow once / Allow this session / Don't allow) for any scope not already granted, holds the user's real OAuth credentials in a Credential Storage the agent never sees, and rejects at an interceptor any tool call falling outside the scope set bound to the agent's session token. The claimed property is trace-level scope containment over tool calls to enrolled services, plus credential isolation from the agent.
advertisedRhetoric: "our enforcement is mechanical and provides rigorous guarantees"; "rigorous security enforcement for tool-calling agents"; "a novel way to automatically and rigorously enforce least privilege principles"; "MiniScope provides rigorous least-privilege guarantees"; and, of the Dual-LLM line of work, it "cannot provide the same rigorous security guarantees as MiniScope". The paper leans once on a cryptographic-strength argument for one leg -- "under the security assumption of the authentication protocol, the probability of an agent correctly guessing a valid credential is negligible" -- but never claims OS-level or cryptographic enforcement of the checker itself. It self-describes architecturally as a proxy: MiniScope "serves as the 'firewall' between the agent and the services." Rhetoric is T1-flavored (rigorous, mechanical, negligible-probability); the described mechanism is an application chokepoint.
tierSpan: We wrap each MCP function with a decorator that validates whether the tool call is permitted under the currently granted permissions.
cheapestDefeat: WORKED TIER DERIVATION. (1) Guarantee: every tool call the agent actually executes on a connected service lies inside the OAuth scope set granted for that session, and the agent never holds the user's bearer token. (2) Mechanism that must fail: the Permission Checker interposed on the agent-to-service path -- implemented as a Python decorator wrapping each MCP function, keyed on a session token carried in the MCP request header, backed by a credential-holding forwarding proxy. (3) Cheapest adversary action: reach the effector by any path that never invokes a wrapped MCP function. Nothing in the paper confines the agent process: no sandbox, no seccomp or network namespace, no kernel or hypervisor mechanism, no egress filter, no container is described anywhere. The agent is an ordinary LangGraph Python process on an n2-standard-8 VM. A direct socket open, a local file write, a shell command, or an HTTP call to a service the user never enrolled in MiniScope simply does not traverse the decorator and is therefore neither checked nor logged. Cost: one line of code. (4) A second, strictly in-lane defeat the paper itself concedes: keep every call inside an already-granted scope, which it states it does not detect. With average granted breadth of roughly 30 methods, a single approval buys a large in-scope action budget. (5) The mechanism defeated by the cheapest action is an application-level chokepoint, so the score is T3, NOT T1. The OAuth scopes and session tokens are cryptographic objects, but forging them is unnecessary: the checker is bypassed by an effector path that never calls it. This is exactly the rubric's worked example -- signed capability mandates enforced by an in-process hook score T3. The conservative call is reinforced by an unproven interposition point: the paper says the checker sits between the agent and the services, but the only implementation detail given is a function decorator, and it never states what prevents the agent from originating traffic that bypasses the MCP server entirely.
placementSpan: Such data may contain injection attacks that attempt to mislead the model into performing unintended or harmful actions.

coverageSpans.E1: Requested tool calls are forwarded to the target service using the user’s real credentials only if they are permitted under the granted permissions.
coverageSpans.E2: MiniScope aims to confine potential harm caused by the tool-calling agent to the user’s connected services.
coverageSpans.E3: MiniScope does not provide guarantees against attacks that alter the execution plan within the currently granted permissions.
coverageSpans.E4: MiniScope targets 10 real, widely-used applications: Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Storage, Slack, Dropbox, Outlook, Outlook Calendar, Notion, and Zoom.
coverageSpans.E5: MiniScope targets 10 real, widely-used applications: Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Storage, Slack, Dropbox, Outlook, Outlook Calendar, Notion, and Zoom.
coverageSpans.E6: This design ensures that the agent never directly accesses the user’s actual bearer tokens.
coverageSpans.E7: In this paper, we focus on single agent systems, leaving multi-agent scenarios, where multiple agents communicate on behalf of their users, to future work.

schneider.surrogate: Trace-level scope containment, enforced by an execution monitor: for every step j, every tool call in c_j is permitted under the granted permission state rho_j, where rho_j is the accumulated result of the user's Always-allow / Allow-once / Allow-this-session / Don't-allow decisions. This is a safety property -- every violating prefix is finitely observable at the interceptor and the offending call is refused with an insufficient-permission response -- so it sits inside Schneider's EM-enforceable class, subject to the interposition caveat that the monitor only sees calls routed through the wrapped MCP functions.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is broader and is NOT monitorable: confining potential damage from unreliable LLMs operating over sensitive user services, including the motivating harm that an unreliable agentic system with access to a user's private data may execute tasks misaligned with user intentions or even leak sensitive information. Two components sit outside the enforceable class. (a) Non-leakage of sensitive information is an information-flow hyperproperty -- no single-trace monitor decides it, and MiniScope performs no taint tracking, no IFC, and no argument-level or resource-level analysis (it explicitly defers that to future work in VII-B). (b) Alignment with user intention is not a predicate over the trace at all; it requires knowing intent, which is why the design substitutes the user's live click as an oracle. The paper is honest about the gap between the two halves: it states that it does not directly prevent attacks that attempt to mislead the model into issuing additional tool calls that remain within the same scope. Split, with both halves named.

notes:
WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE CORPUS (the mobile-permission analogy). MiniScope is the cleanest instance in the corpus of an authorization layer that imports the mobile-OS permission idiom wholesale -- the four-button dialog (Always allow / Allow once / Allow this session / Don't allow), the per-scope description string, the revoke-it-later-in-settings affordance -- citing Android's permission documentation directly and adapting it to the agentic setting. The idiom carries a binding expectation it cannot honor here. On Android the grant is enforced by the kernel and the framework: a denied app cannot reach the camera by spawning a helper process, opening a raw socket, or writing to a path it was not given. Here the identical dialog is backed by a Python decorator on an MCP function inside an unconfined process. Same UI grammar, two tiers apart in what the click actually binds. That mismatch is the finding, not a criticism of the engineering -- the ILP formulation and the reconstructed OAuth hierarchies are genuinely new, and the six overprivileged real-world ChatGPT/Claude connector configurations the solver surfaces are a real empirical result.

TIER. Scored T3 conservatively. The paper never claims OS or cryptographic enforcement of the checker, but its rhetoric (rigorous, mechanical, negligible probability) reads at T1, and a reader may take the OAuth substrate to be doing the binding. It is not: the scopes bind what the SERVICE accepts from a token, which is real and does raise the floor -- an agent that never obtains a bearer token cannot mint calls against Gmail at all. That credential isolation is the strongest genuine property in the paper and deserves credit. But it binds only the enrolled-service lane, and it is defeated the moment the effector is reachable off that lane. Advertised tier recorded as unclear rather than T1 because the paper's own architectural self-description (a firewall between the agent and the services) is a T3 description; the T1 flavor lives in the adjectives, not the mechanism.

INTERPOSITION POINT IS PARTIALLY UNPROVEN. Per the stance rule, the only concrete interposition detail given is the function decorator. The session token travels in the MCP request header to the MCP server, which suggests the decorator lives server-side (better than in-agent), but the paper never states this, never states what stops the agent from reaching a service directly, and never describes a network chokepoint. Treated as unproven and scored at the weaker reading.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT -- UNCERTAINTY FLAGGED. The rubric asks for the placement the evaluation actually tests. NO ADVERSARIAL EVALUATION EXISTS IN THIS PAPER. The three evaluation questions are permission minimality versus an LLM baseline, runtime overhead, and user-confirmation frequency. Figure 5's in-scope attack that can be detected by MiniScope is an illustration, not an experiment; no attack suite is run, no bypass is attempted, no injection corpus is executed. Primary is therefore recorded as A2 -- the narrower, concretely illustrated adversary (indirect prompt injection via the data section of the prompt and via untrusted tool responses; the running example is a customer-support message containing an instruction to ignore prior instructions and delete all emails). A3 is listed secondary and is arguably co-primary: the formal security game hands the adversary the model outright (the adversary chooses f_LLM and the set of valid states M for all services, and the paper makes no trust assumptions about the underlying LLM used by the agent), and the checker is source-agnostic so it covers A3 by construction. A1 secondary (attacker seeding service state through legitimate API calls). A4 secondary and only half-addressed: the Least Privilege Solver is a LangGraph node INSIDE the agent graph, so a harness-resident adversary can submit a benign plan; the paper anticipates exactly this and blocks the credential-theft variant via the proxy, but an A4 adversary that simply does not use MCP is untouched. A5 is not addressed at all.

COVERAGE REASONING, CELL BY CELL.
E1 file write = partial. MiniScope genuinely mediates remote file mutation through Google Drive, Dropbox and Google Storage scopes at the MCP chokepoint (its own audit finds a Drive scope enabling file modification and deletion beyond stated read-only behavior). It does not touch the local filesystem, rename, or unlink at all, and within-scope writes are conceded unmediated. ADJUDICATOR NOTE: if the corpus scopes E1 to the LOCAL filesystem only, this cell should be not-covered rather than partial. I coded partial because cloud-object mutation is a genuine instance of the effector class and is provably reached at the assigned tier for enrolled services.
E2 subprocess spawn = not-covered. The paper contains no notion of a process, a child process, or a shell. There is nothing to bypass because nothing exists; the depth rule is moot since there is no top-level mediation to cap.
E3 network egress = partial. Egress to enrolled services is mediated (that is the whole product); arbitrary egress from the agent or anything it launches is not, and no descendant egress is mediated, which independently caps the ceiling at partial under the depth rule. Also capped by the covert-channel rule: exfiltration achieved inside a granted scope (for example a permitted send or share method) is explicitly excluded from the contract, and honest exclusion does not close the channel.
E4 VCS push = not-covered. No version-control service appears among the ten targets; Google Storage is object storage, not a VCS. One could imagine reconstructing a GitHub scope hierarchy, but coverage records what the system delivers, not what it could be pointed at.
E5 package install = not-covered. Install hooks and their network activity are never mentioned; there is no package manager anywhere in the model.
E6 credential use = partial, and this is MiniScope's strongest cell. Real property: the agent never receives the user's bearer tokens; the proxy attaches them after the check passes. But the E6 rule caps at partial absent a published credential list, and MiniScope publishes only a per-service OAuth scope map for its enrolled services. It says nothing about environment variables, config files, OS keychains, or cloud instance-metadata endpoints reachable from the same unconfined process -- any of which would let the agent obtain credentials outside the Credential Storage entirely. Partial, capped both by rule and by fact.
E7 sub-agent spawn = not-covered, by the authors' own explicit deferral of multi-agent scenarios to future work.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2, WITH A CAVEAT AN ADJUDICATOR MUST SEE. The L2 is earned by the mechanism, not by the security claim: roughly 8,000 lines of Python, a working LangGraph plus MCP end-to-end agent, measured 1-6% latency overhead with permission-solving and checking broken out as separate components, ILP solutions computed across ten real applications, a simulated three-month interaction study on Gmail, and a real-world audit finding six overprivileged connector configurations. All of that behaviorally confirms that the enforcement path runs and refuses out-of-scope calls. NONE of it behaviorally confirms bypass resistance, because no bypass was attempted. If the corpus grades evidence strictly against the stated security guarantee rather than against the artifact, this should be read as L1-plus rather than a clean L2.

SECONDARY OBSERVATION WORTH KEEPING. The paper's own finding that OAuth scope NAMES do not track scope SEMANTICS (the naming hierarchy of scopes does not necessarily reflect their actual functional hierarchy; Mail.Read appears to be a child node of Mail.ReadWrite but in fact is not) is a strong independent argument that human-readable permission dialogs mislead users even when the underlying grant is honest -- which sharpens the mobile-analogy critique rather than weakening it. It also means the user clicking the mobile-style button is being asked to adjudicate a hierarchy the paper has just shown to be counterintuitive even to its designers.
